entities.summary:
Angelotto Fosco (b. 1378, Rome – September 21, 1444), an influential Italian cardinal and bishop, navigated the complex ecclesiastical and political landscape of 15th-century Rome and the Papal States. His career, spanning the Great Western Schism and its aftermath, positioned him as a significant figure in the Roman Curia, impacting papal administration, patronage, and the broader spiritual and temporal governance of the late Medieval Church. His strategic loyalty and administrative acumen were crucial in an era defined by institutional strife and the nascent stirrings of the Renaissance.

Fosco's ascent began with his appointment as Bishop of Todi in 1418 by Pope Martin V, a crucial period following the Council of Constance and the reunification of the papacy. He quickly distinguished himself as a capable administrator, serving as a papal nuncio and demonstrating both fiscal acumen and diplomatic skill in managing Church affairs. His elevation to cardinal by Pope Eugene IV in 1431 marked him as a key supporter during a tumultuous papacy, particularly amidst the challenges posed by the Council of Basel and the Roman uprising of 1434. Fosco remained steadfastly loyal to Eugene IV, even enduring exile from Rome alongside the pontiff, highlighting his commitment to papal authority during a period of intense conciliarism.

His legacy primarily rests on his contributions to the restoration of papal power and financial stability after decades of schism and conflict. Fosco's administrative capabilities helped streamline curial operations and manage the Church's extensive temporal holdings, providing a crucial framework for future papal governance. His patronage of the arts and architecture, typical of high-ranking prelates of his time, also contributed to Rome's early Renaissance cultural revival, laying groundwork for the city's eventual transformation into a center of artistic and intellectual endeavor.
